notes.meaning: Elihu calls Job directly by his personal name and asks for his full attention. The three older friends had never addressed Job by name during their long debates. Elihu asks Job to listen to everything he has to say before making up his mind.

Elihu announces that he is ready to speak and that his thoughts are already formed. He uses the image of the mouth and tongue testing words like tasting food. He wants Job to know that he has weighed his words carefully rather than speaking in a rush.

Elihu promises that his speech will come from an honest and sincere heart. Unlike the older friends, he claims he will not twist facts out of anger or personal bias. He intends to speak clearly and plainly so Job can easily understand him.

Elihu reminds Job that God's Spirit created him and gave him life. He shares the same human origin that God gave to Adam at the creation of the world. Because God made both of them, Elihu can speak as a fellow creature who has been given reason and understanding.

differ.view: Some Baptists emphasize this verse as clear proof of the divine personhood and creating power of the Holy Spirit, while also seeing Elihu's life as a picture of spiritual rebirth.

notes.meaning: Elihu invites Job to answer him and organize his arguments like a lawyer in a courtroom. He gives Job full liberty to defend his case. He wants a fair discussion rather than an unequal argument.

Elihu explains that before God, he is a frail human being just like Job. Both of them were formed by God out of common clay. Job had repeatedly wished for an umpire or advocate he could speak with without fear, and Elihu offers himself as that fellow man.

Elihu reassures Job that he does not need to be terrified of him. Job had feared that God's great majesty would crush him if they met in court. Since Elihu is only human, his presence will not overwhelm Job, and his words will not be heavy or cruel.

Elihu states that he heard Job's complaints with his own ears. He is not relying on second-hand reports, rumors, or guesswork. Because Job spoke these things out loud, Elihu feels responsible to answer them directly.

Elihu summarizes Job as claiming to be entirely clean, innocent, and free from all sin. While Job had firmly defended his integrity against his friends' false charges, he had never actually claimed to be sinless. Elihu overstates Job's words, making his complaints sound much more extreme than they really were.

Elihu reminds Job of his complaint that God was searching for reasons to oppose him. Job had felt in his deep grief that God was treating him like an enemy. Elihu points out how dangerous it is to accuse God of looking for excuses to attack His people.

Elihu repeats Job's earlier complaint that God had locked his feet in stocks and watched every step he took. Job had felt trapped and treated like a criminal on trial. Elihu highlights these harsh words to show Job how bitter his speech had become.

Elihu tells Job plainly that he is in the wrong because God is far greater than man. God is not merely stronger than humans; He is also infinitely greater in justice, holiness, and wisdom. For a weak and limited creature to accuse such a God of acting unfairly is completely wrong.

Elihu asks Job why he demands an explanation from God as if God were on trial. God is the sovereign ruler over all things and does not owe any creature an explanation for His actions. Complaining against God's silence is foolish because He does what is right even when we cannot see His reasons.

Elihu argues that God does indeed speak to people, and does so in more than one way. The problem is not that God is silent, but that people fail to notice or understand His voice. God repeats His warnings patiently so that sinners are left without excuse.

Elihu describes the first way God speaks: through dreams and night visions while people are asleep in bed. In the quiet hours of the night, when the senses are shut off from daily distractions, the human heart is more open to divine impressions. In Bible times, before the written Scriptures were complete, God often used dreams to deliver important messages.

differ.view: Charismatic Christians believe that God continues to speak directly through supernatural dreams and night visions today to guide and warn believers.

notes.meaning: When God gives these night messages, He opens people's spiritual ears so they will pay attention. He seals His instruction into their minds like a seal stamped into warm wax. This means God's warnings leave a deep and lasting mark upon the conscience.

God sends these warnings to turn people away from their bad plans and to keep them from pride. Pride makes people stubborn in doing evil, so God cuts it down before it ruins them. His warnings are not meant to destroy people, but to protect them from their own sinful choices.

differ.view: Reformed Christians see this verse as showing how God uses painful warnings and trials to uncover hidden remnants of pride even in upright believers, leading them to deeper humility and faith.

notes.meaning: The goal of God's warning is to keep a person's soul from the pit of death and destruction. A guilty life heading toward ruin is stopped by the mercy of an awakened conscience. By turning a sinner away from sin, God saves him from sudden physical death and eternal judgment.

Elihu presents a second way God speaks to people: through physical sickness and deep, constant pain in the bones. When soft warnings do not work, God uses bodily suffering to get a person's attention. This suffering is not just punishment, but a loving discipline meant to train and heal the soul.

The sick person becomes so ill that he completely loses his appetite for ordinary bread. Even the finest and tastiest foods make him feel sick to his stomach. This loss of physical desire shows how deeply illness breaks down human strength and earthly pleasures.

Severe illness causes the patient's body to waste away until he looks like skin and bones. Flesh that was once full and healthy vanishes, and bones that used to be hidden now stick out sharply. This stark picture matched Job's own miserable physical state.

The suffering person sinks so low that he comes to the very edge of the grave. He faces the messengers of death, meaning the final pangs that bring an end to life. Human help is useless at this point, and only God can turn him back from the grave.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars note that the phrase 'messengers of death' may reflect ancient Near Eastern ideas about death-dealing spirits who carried people away to the underworld.

notes.meaning: A dying person can be rescued if a special messenger or interpreter—one in a thousand—comes to his side. This mediator explains God's purpose in the suffering and teaches the man how to walk in uprightness and humble faith. Christian commentators have long seen this rare mediator as a picture of Jesus Christ, who alone represents God to man and man to God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern commentators read the messenger as a heavenly angel from God's council or an exceptionally wise human teacher, without seeing a direct reference to Christ.

notes.meaning: God shows mercy to the dying person and commands that he be rescued from going down to the pit. The reason for this rescue is that God has found a ransom. A ransom is the price paid to deliver a captive, which Christians understand as the atonement made by Jesus Christ on the cross to save sinners from eternal death.

Once the ransom is applied, the sick person's body begins to heal and his skin becomes as fresh as a little child's. His strength returns, and he feels young again. This physical healing is an outward sign of the spiritual renewal and fresh start God gives to forgiven sinners.

The restored person prays to God and is accepted with delight, seeing God's face with great joy. The cloud of fear is gone, and he enjoys peace with his Maker. God treats him as righteous and gives him the gladness of being restored to fellowship.

The healed person openly confesses his past before other people and sings praises to God. He honestly admits that he sinned and twisted what was right, but acknowledges that God did not punish him as he deserved. True repentance always includes confessing wrongdoing and praising God's unearned mercy.

The redeemed man continues his praise, declaring that God delivered his soul from the dark pit of the grave. He rejoices that he is still alive to see the light of day and the light of God's favor. His deliverance gives him lasting hope and deep gratitude.

Elihu explains that God does all these things repeatedly—two or even three times—for human beings. God is very patient and does not give up after a single warning is ignored. He uses dreams, pain, and messengers over and over to draw sinners back to Himself.

God's great purpose in all these trials is to turn a person's soul back from death and destruction. He wants the rescued sinner to live in the light of the living and enjoy true happiness. Affliction is not God's way of destroying people, but His loving tool to save them from ruin.

Elihu asks Job to pay very close attention to what he is saying and to stay silent for a moment. He wants Job to take these truths to heart instead of reacting quickly. Elihu believes he is offering a helpful explanation that Job needs to hear completely.

Elihu invites Job to speak up if he has any genuine answer or objection to offer. He says he would be glad to see Job cleared and vindicated if possible. Unlike the older friends who wanted to prove Job guilty, Elihu says he is searching for the truth and hopes Job can be found upright.

If Job has no answer to make, Elihu urges him to remain quiet so he can teach him true wisdom. Since Job stays silent and does not reply, Elihu prepares to continue his speech. He believes God has given him insight into how trials work for a person's good.
